2.1 Junction Introduction

Objectives

By the end of Topic 2, you shall be able to:

  • Identify the characteristics of different types of at-grade junctions.
  • Justify the choice of junction types based on given requirements and constraints.
  • Perform preliminary design of priority junction, roundabout, and traffic signal junction.
  • Analyze the capacity of priority junction, roundabout, and traffic signal junction using manual calculation and design software.

4 major sections

  1. Introduction: Types of junctions, comparison
  2. Design of at-grade junctions
  3. Priority Junction
  4. Roundabout
  5. Traffic Signal

(The slide lists them as 1. Introduction, then Design of at-grade junctions, then 2. Priority Junction, 3. Roundabout, 4. Traffic Signal. The numbering is slightly inconsistent; the above reflects the intended structure.)

Traffic Network

  • Network: Nodes and links
  • Links: Roads of different types
  • Nodes: Various land use / activity locations or Junctions
Key Idea

A traffic network is made up of links (roads) and nodes (junctions, terminals, land uses).

Road Types in Hong Kong

Expressway

  • Roads designated as Expressways under the Road Traffic (Expressway) Regulations.
  • An expressway may be formed from a trunk road or a primary distributor road.

Urban Roads (Kowloon, Hong Kong Island, New Town)

Urban Roads (Kowloon, Hong Kong Island, New Town)

Trunk Roads (UT)
  • Roads connecting the main centres of population.
  • High-capacity roads.
  • No frontage access or development.
  • Segregation of pedestrians.
  • Widely spaced grade-separated junctions.
  • 24-hour stopping restrictions.
Primary Distributor (PD)
  • Roads forming the major network of the urban area.
  • High-capacity junctions, though may be at-grade.
  • Segregated pedestrian facilities wherever possible.
  • Frontage access limited if not entirely restricted.
  • 2-hour stopping restrictions.
District Distributor (DD)
  • Roads linking Districts to the Primary Distributor Roads.
  • High capacity at-grade junctions.
  • Peak hour stopping restrictions.
  • Parking restrictions throughout the day.
Local Distributor (LD)
  • Roads within Districts linking developments to the District Distributor Roads.

Rural Roads (New Territories outside of New Towns)

Rural Roads (New Territories outside of New Towns)

Trunk Roads (RT)
  • Roads connecting the main centres of population.
  • High-capacity roads.
  • No frontage access or development.
  • Pedestrians segregated.
  • Widely spaced grade-separated junctions.
  • 24-hour stopping restrictions.
Rural Roads (RR)
  • Roads connecting the smaller centres of population or popular recreation areas with major road networks.
  • Frontage access should be limited wherever possible.
  • Junction design, whilst not necessarily grade separated, should be of a high-capacity standard.
Feeder Roads
  • Roads connecting villages or more remote settlements to Rural Roads.

Topic 2.1 Junctions — Part 2 Summary Notes

Scope

This note covers the Junctions section (Part 2). It includes the definition of junctions, traffic conflicts, weaving, junction goals, control strategies, and terminology.

2.2 Junction

1. Junctions (or Intersections): inevitable part of any street system

  • The general area where two or more roads join or cross, including the roadway and roadside facilities for traffic movement within it.
  • A junction has to be shared by everybody who wants to use it (vehicles, pedestrians).
  • Needs to be designed with great care:
    • Safety >>> capacity, efficiency, speed, cost of operation…

Goal

  • Control and manage conflict (vehicle–vehicle, vehicle–pedestrian).
  • Safety, efficiency, delay… (and other constraints).

Process

Choice of Junction Type
→
Junction Design (and configuration)

Traffic Conflicts

Conflict Type Description
MergingVehicles enter a traffic stream
DivergingVehicles leave traffic stream
WeavingVehicles cross paths by first merging and then diverging
CrossingVehicles cross paths directly
Key Idea

All four conflict types occur at junctions, and the goal of junction design is to control and manage these conflicts.

More about "weaving"

  • Weaving movements cross each other's path.
  • Types of weaving segments:
    • (a) One-Sided Ramp-Weave
    • (b) One-Sided Major Weave
    • (c) Two-Sided Weaving Segment w/ Single-Lane Ramps
    • (d) Two-Sided Weaving Segment w/ Three Lane Changes
  • Weaving also occurs at roundabouts.
  • Real-world examples show merge and diverge points on highways.

How much freedom the driver has vs How much control the traffic agency exercises

More driver
freedom
More agency
control
Passive Control

No Control (Rules of the Road):

  • Right-of-way is not explicitly assigned.
  • Follow driving convention ("Basic Rules of the Road"), such as through movement has higher priority than turning movement.

Traffic Signs (plus road marking) to regulate, warn, and guide traffic, e.g. stop and yield signs.

Semi Control

Drivers are gently guided to avoid conflicts.

  • Channelization
  • Roundabout: through and right-turn traffic forced to move around the central circle in clockwise direction. Convert crossing conflict into merging → weaving → diverging.
Active Control

Road users are forced to follow the path suggested by the traffic control agencies.

  • Traffic Signal: at a given time, only certain traffic movements are permitted to pass through the intersection.
  • Grade separated intersections: Eliminate the crossing conflict by placing conflicting traffic streams at different elevations at their point of intersection.

TERMINOLOGY

Approach and Lane

  • Approach: A lane or a group of lanes through which traffic enters intersection.
  • Nearside lane: The lane that is the furthest from the road median.
  • Farside lane: The lane that is the closest to the road median.
  • Eastbound Approach: Eastbound = travelling towards the east.
  • Westbound Approach: Westbound = travelling towards the west.

Diagram reference: The slide shows a typical cross intersection with eastbound and westbound approaches, nearside and farside lanes, stop lines, and various road markings.

Single and Dual Carriageway

  • Single: without central divider.
  • Dual: with central divider.

Central divider (also called Central Reserve)

  • Separate traffic flows in opposite direction.
  • Provide freedom from interference from opposing traffic.
  • Improve speed and safety.

Single Carriageway

  • Lane changing by getting into opposing traffic lanes is possible.

Diagram reference: The slide shows typical cross-sections for a Primary Distributor Road (dual carriageway with central reserve) and a single carriageway road with footways, verges, and road markings.

Topic 2.1 Junctions — Part 3 Summary Notes

Scope

This note covers the Types of Junction section (Part 3). It includes the junction types and control strategy table (carried over from Part 2), then details of at-grade intersections and grade-separated interchanges.

Types of Junction

Junction Types & Junction Control Strategy — Summary Table

Junction Type Control Strategy
Uncontrolled IntersectionNo Control, "rules of the road"
ChannelizationSeparation/regulation of conflicting movements into definite paths
Priority JunctionOne of the intersecting roads is given definite priority over the other
RoundaboutSpace Sharing, i.e. intend to permit fully equal priority and continuous movement for all intersecting vehicle flows
Traffic SignalTime Sharing, i.e. assign right of way to alternative streams at different point in time
InterchangeGrade Separation, i.e. eliminate the crossing conflict by placing conflicting traffic streams at different elevations at their point of intersection

Increasing order of control exercised at junctions:

Uncontrolled Intersection
→
Channelization
→
Priority Junction
→
Roundabout
→
Traffic Signal

Two main categories:

  • At grade: Two or more highways join, each highway radiating from or forming part of the intersection.
  • Grade-separated: Highways cross each other at a different grade, with no connection.

1. Uncontrolled Intersection

  • No control devices.
  • Visibility distance is critical.
  • The operator of a vehicle approaching an intersection must be able to perceive a hazard in sufficient time to alter the vehicle's speed, as necessary, before reaching the intersection.
  • Design criteria involved: Safety, efficiency, speed, cost of operation, and capacity.

Design check for uncontrolled intersection

  • Locate vehicle A (usually on minor road) at stopping distance (ISD) from the collision point.
  • Determine the actual location of vehicle B when drivers first see each other (by geometry, using location of the obstruction).
  • Check whether the actual distance between vehicle B and the collision point is longer than its stopping distance (ISD).
  • ISD > stopping distance?

Stopping distance formula

2. Channelization

  • Separation or regulation of conflicting traffic movements into definite paths of travel by traffic islands or pavement markings to facilitate the safe and orderly movements of both vehicles and pedestrians.
  • Benefits:
    • Improve safety
    • Maximizes convenience
    • Instills drivers' confidence
  • Can be used alone or supplement other control measures (e.g. priority junction, roundabout, …).
  • Diagram reference: The slide shows examples of channelized intersections with islands and markings.

3. Priority Junction

  • Traffic on the major road has continual priority over the traffic on the minor road.
  • Minor road traffic is controlled by:
    • "Stop" or "Give Way" signs
    • Associated carriageway markings
  • The onus is entirely on the minor road traffic to decide when it is safe to enter the major road.

Stop Signs

  • "Stop" is placed on a minor road at its junction with a major road.
  • A vehicle must stop at the transverse lines or, if the transverse lines are not present, the vehicle must still stop at the major road.
  • The vehicle should not proceed into the major road in a manner or at a time that would cause danger to the driver of a vehicle on the major road or cause that vehicle to change its direction or speed.

Yield Signs (Give Way)

  • "Give Way" is placed on minor roads at their junctions with major roads.
  • The vehicle on the minor road should not enter the major road, in such a manner or at such a time, as to cause danger to a vehicle on the major road or cause the driver of such a vehicle to change its speed or direction.

Diagram reference: The slide shows stop sign and give way sign markings (Road User's Code).

4. Roundabout

  • Considered as a form of channelized priority junction.
  • Vehicles enter a one-way carriageway and move in a clockwise direction around a central island (or anticlockwise direction, depending on the country's driving rules).
  • Entering vehicles give priority to those vehicles already circulating across their entry.
  • Variations: signalized roundabout, grade-separated roundabout.

Diagram reference: The slide shows an aerial view of a roundabout.

5. Traffic Signal

  • The traffic signal is an electrically timed device.
  • It assigns the right-of-way to one or more traffic streams so that these traffic streams can pass through the intersection safely and efficiently.
  • Utilizes time-sharing operation.
  • Traffic streams are allowed to enter the junction for a period of time, indicated by an illuminated signal, and during which period conflicting traffic streams are halted.

Diagram reference: The slide shows a traffic signal head.

6. Interchange

  • All previous types of junctions are at-grade intersections.
  • Interchange resolves traffic conflicts by grade separation.
  • Advantages:
    • Increased capacity
    • Less vehicular delay
    • Fewer accidents
    • Reduced operating costs
  • Disadvantages:
    • High construction costs
    • Usually increased land intake

Diagram reference: The slide shows an aerial view of a multi-level interchange and schematic diagrams of various interchange types.

Interchange types:

Interchange Type Description Key Features Hong Kong Example
Trumpet Interchange Single bridge structure carrying the minor road above the major road.
  • Lower volume has to use the loop.
  • One of the intersecting legs is approximately prolongation of the direction approach of another.
 Queensway / Justice Drive Flyover [Admiralty]
Diamond Interchange Simplest four-way, two-level junction.
  • Single bridge and four one-way ramps.
  • Only narrow area is required, particularly suitable for use in urban areas.
  • Conflicts can occur at the points where the slip roads meet the crossing minor roads.
 Tuen Mun Rd / Tuen Hing Rd Interchange
Elevated Main Route Major route is carried on bridge structure over the minor route.
  • A basic principle in the design of grade separated interchanges is that the minor route should be carried above the major route.
  • Reason for elevated main route: More economical and the advantage of providing accelerating traffic with a down gradient and decelerating traffic with an up gradient.
  • Application: New major routes in existing urban areas.
 Kwai Tsing Interchange [Kwai Chung]
Cloverleaf Interchange Four-way, two-level.
  • No terminal right-turns at-grade.
  • Right-turn by loop slip roads, all left-turn movements.
  • Do not need traffic signals on the crossing highway.
  • Very large land intake.
 N / A
Partial Cloverleaf Interchange Accommodating a junction within a space constrained by existing development.
  • The quadrant in which the ramps are located can be varied to suit the site restrictions.
 Po Kong Village Rd / Lung Cheung Rd
Elevated Roundabout Multiway Junction.
  • Useful when the intersection has more than four approach arms.
  • Main highway underpassing or overpassing an at-grade roundabout junction.
  • Frees the movement of the major through traffic stream.
  • Minor and interchanging traffic confined to the roundabout.
 Lei Yue Mun Rd Interchange [Lam Tin]

Topic 2.1 Junctions — Part 4 Summary Notes

Scope

This note covers Choice of Junction Types. It includes considerations for selecting junction types, junction capacity, delay characteristics, safety, economic considerations, pedestrian considerations, and other factors, ending with summary tables.

Choice of Junction Types

  • At-grade: Priority Junction, Roundabout, Signal Junction
  • Grade Separated Interchange
  • Will not be discussed extensively.

Considerations:

  • Capacity, Delay, Safety, Economic Considerations, Pedestrians
  • + Environmental and topographical considerations
  • + Consistency with surrounding road network
  • E.g., on high-speed roads, traffic signals which require abrupt changes of speed should be avoided.
  • Roundabout should be avoided in an area which is controlled by Area Traffic Control (area-wide control of traffic signals).

1. Junction Capacity

Design Flow
Input parameter. The traffic volume we anticipate the junction needs to handle.

Junction Capacity
The level of vehicle that a junction can (reasonably) handle (acceptable delay).

Delay

  • Junction operating close to (or above) capacity ⇒ longer delay.
  • Some approaches may experience more delay than other approaches.

General order of junction capacity

In general, junction capacity approximately follows this order:

Grade Separated Interchange
>
Roundabout
≈
Traffic Signal
>
Priority (Give Way)
  • No hard and fast rule in choosing junction type according to design flow.

Approximate priority junction provision on single carriageway roads based on flows only

We will come back to this chart later.

1. Design Flow (for all junction types)

In designing and evaluating all junction types it is necessary to predict design flows, which should be:

  1. Peak hour volumes.
  2. For a future year not less than 10 years after scheme implementation.
  3. Consider fluctuations and uncertainty.
  • The junction design needs to provide adequate capacity to handle the predicted flows in the design year.
  • Details: TPDM Vol 2 Ch 4.4.2.4

Design Flow – Catering for variation

  • To cater for variation, design for the maximum instead of average flow.
  • Hourly, daily and seasonal variation.
  • Based on highest expected design flow, especially for those infrequently occurred peaks, so that the designed junction control would be able to cater for the heaviest traffic flow condition.
  • In some cases, the design flow may be considerably higher than the average future flow predicted by modelling techniques.
  • Unexpected, short-term variation: add some safety margin.
  • Where short duration queuing is expected to be a particular problem, allowance should also be made, in deriving the design flow, for short term variation within the peak hour.
  • For manual calculation of capacities (priority junctions and roundabouts), it is suggested that an increase of 10–15% be applied to the peak hour flows to allow for this occurrence.
Simple Explanation of Design Flow – Catering for variation
  • Design for the busiest case, not the average.
    • Traffic varies by hour, day, and season. The junction must handle the heaviest flow that could reasonably occur.
  • Add a safety margin.
    • For short-term fluctuations within the peak hour, add about 10–15% to the peak hour flow, especially for manual capacity calculations.
  • Why?
    • To ensure the junction still works well even when traffic is unexpectedly high.

Example of data in Appendix H_Annual Traffic Census

Delay Considerations

Delay Type Explanation
Delay – Priority Junction • Delays experienced only by the minor road traffic.
• Major road traffic flows virtually unimpeded.
• Heavier major road traffic → longer delay for minor traffic.
• Long delays encourage smaller gap acceptance → increase in accidents.
• Need capacity/delay analysis.
Delay – Traffic Signal • Can distribute delay fairly — no particular movement suffers disproportionate delays.
• At low flow levels, total delay increases compared with a priority layout.
• Delays can be minimised by linking adjacent signal-controlled junctions (signal coordination).
• Need capacity/delay analysis.
Delay – Roundabout • With well-balanced flows, delays minimised over a full range of flow up to levels close to capacity.
• Problems arise with single predominant flows causing long delays.
• Need capacity/delay analysis.

Safety Considerations

Junction Type Safety Explanation
Priority Junction High accident rate • High difference in speed between through and turning traffic.
• Total dependence on the judgment of minor road drivers to determine a safe gap in the major road traffic stream.
Roundabouts Less severe accidents than other at-grade junction types • Low vehicle speeds when entering roundabout.
Traffic Signal Low accident rate • Positive indication provided to drivers.
• Rear end accidents usually increase.
• Vehicles stopping suddenly when lights change.

Economics Considerations

  • Cost vs benefits
    • Costs: construction costs, land costs etc.
    • Benefits: reduced delay and accidents, etc.
  • How do "priority junction", "traffic signal junction", "roundabout" and "interchange" compare in construction cost/land cost?
  • Cost: staged construction
    • Delaying construction of part of a junction layout until traffic volumes increase sufficiently to warrant the more extensive design.
  • Diagram: Priority Junction → (as traffic increases) can evolve to Signal Control or Roundabout. (Why? – not stated in slide but implied due to capacity needs.)

Pedestrian Considerations

The needs of pedestrians are no less important than the needs of vehicular traffic in junction design.

Forecasts of future pedestrian demand:

  • Adequate capacity and minimum delay for pedestrians.
  • Safety.
  • Elderly, disabled persons, people who require mobility aids.
Priority Junctions
  • Easy for pedestrians to negotiate.
  • Use guard-railing to indicate intended crossing place.
  • Physical islands give refuge — cross one direction of traffic at a time.
  • As pedestrian volumes increase, add controlled crossings on one or more arms.
Traffic Signals
  • Safest and most efficient way to handle pedestrians at-grade.
  • Even with light pedestrian flow, pedestrians can still cross traffic streams.
  • Where justified, separate pedestrian phases give a positive signal to cross.
  • Green Man Crossings are an example.
Roundabouts
  • Least appropriate at-grade junction for pedestrians (unless on a segregated network).
  • Flared approaches make siting crossings difficult.
  • Crossings often placed further back from the give way line, where the road is narrower.
  • Consider subways and/or footbridges for heavy pedestrian demand.

Other considerations

  • Environmental and topographical considerations
  • Consistency with the surrounding road network:
    • E.g. roundabout should be avoided in an area which is controlled by Area Traffic Control (signal synchronization).
    • Similarly on high-speed roads, traffic signals which require abrupt changes of speed should be avoided.

Table 4.2.9.1 – Summary of Junction Types

Design Parameter Priority Junction Traffic Signal Junction Roundabout Junction Grade Separated Junction
Capacity Low – moderate flows Moderate – high flows Moderate – high flows High flows
Delay Long delays for minor road at high flows Fair distribution; can coordinate; some delay at low flow Little delay if under capacity; problems with dominant flow No delay to major through traffic; little to minor turns
Safety High accident rate; relies on driver judgement Low accident rate; rear-end accidents increase Safest at-grade; low speeds Fewest conflicts; severe accidents at high speed
Economic Very low construction cost; land take may be costly Very cost effective; equipment offset by land savings May be expensive due to land take High cost; offset by community benefits
Pedestrian OK for small simple junctions; avoid shadow islands with heavy flow Best at-grade option; positive indication Least appropriate; diverse unattractive routes Grade separated pedestrian facilities required
